analysis.one_liner: Sets binding limits on toxic heavy metals like arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury in baby food.
analysis.headline: The bill set enforceable limits for arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury in food for children under 3, won 29 Democratic sponsors, and never received a committee vote before the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make infant and toddler food legally adulterated if it exceeds set limits on toxic heavy metals: 10 parts per billion for inorganic arsenic (15 for cereal), 5 for cadmium, 5 for lead, and 2 for mercury. It requires manufacturers to test their products and publish the results twice a year, lets the FDA force a recall of baby food exceeding the limits, and directs the CDC to run a public awareness campaign. The FDA would review the levels and tighten them over time, and $50 million would fund research on farming methods that keep heavy metals out of crops. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, where it stayed without action until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Parents and young children, who would get legally enforceable maximum levels of toxic metals in the food babies eat, plus published test results so families can see what is in products before buying. Children's developing brains are most vulnerable to arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury exposure.

how_it_helps.text: Food for children up to 36 months would be deemed adulterated if it exceeds specific action levels: 10 parts per billion for inorganic arsenic (15 for cereal), 5 for cadmium, 5 for lead, and 2 for mercury, with the FDA required to review and lower the levels over time. [S3]
Facilities making infant and toddler food would have to run testing programs, verify their controls work, and publish a report of their monitoring and test results online every six months. [S3]
The FDA's mandatory recall power would be extended to baby food that exceeds the toxic-element limits, replacing reliance on voluntary recalls. [S2] [S3]
The CDC would run a public awareness campaign on the risks of toxic elements in baby food, and $50 million would go to research on farming methods that minimize heavy metals in crops. [S2] [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Baby food manufacturers bear the cost of testing, reformulating products and tightening sourcing to meet the limits. Farms and ingredient suppliers whose crops absorb heavy metals from soil, notably rice growers, would face pressure to change varieties, fields or processing, and some products could be pulled from shelves.
analysis.who_pays_short: Baby food makers and heavy-metal-absorbing crops

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would be passed into prices for a product families buy daily, and the fixed starting limits were set by statute rather than by the FDA's own risk assessment, which critics said could force removal of products faster than suppliers could adjust. [S3]

Heavy metals in food come partly from soil and water that growers cannot fully control, so the burden falls on agricultural producers and could raise prices or reduce supply of some baby foods, especially cereals. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: infants are the population most sensitive to neurotoxic metals, and today there is no binding legal limit for arsenic, lead, cadmium or mercury in baby food. The costs fall on a concentrated manufacturing sector and some farm suppliers, and the fixed numeric limits written directly into the bill would have worked better with a phase-in. On balance, the bill's protections for a uniquely vulnerable group outweigh the compliance costs it would impose.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee in March 2021 and sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 26, 2021 by Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. [S5]
Three days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where the committee action record ends. [S5]
No further action, hearing, markup, or vote is listed; the last entry in the bill's action history remains the subcommittee referral. [S5]
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill expired with a single referral and no vote in either chamber. [S1] [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Baby food manufacturers and ingredient suppliers are better off, since they avoid testing, reformulation and recall obligations that no other law imposed. Parents remain without a binding legal limit on toxic metals in the food babies eat.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Baby food manufacturers, spared new testing rules

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican signed on, and the Democratic-controlled committee was the body that declined to act.

industries.note: The bill would require toxic-metal testing, published results twice a year, compliance with binding limits, and recall exposure — direct new costs for a handful of large producers. Those costs are the mechanism by which babies' food gets safer, so the industry's interest in this bill runs against parents'.

industries.industry: Rice and grain growers and ingredient suppliers
industries.note: Heavy metals enter baby food mainly through crops grown in contaminated soil and water, especially rice. Binding limits would force growers to change varieties, fields or processing, or find their crops shut out of the baby food supply.
Mandatory environmental and finished-product testing programs would create a new, guaranteed market for heavy-metal testing services.
